title: World CO2 Emissions by Energy Type (Electricity & Heat Generation)
description: Global electricity generation mix and the CO2 emissions attributable to the power (electricity & heat) sector, broken down by primary energy source -- coal, natural gas, oil -- with renewables and nuclear noted as near-zero direct-emission sources. This is distinct from co2_by_fuel_type.json, which uses the Global Carbon Project's economy-wide fuel categories (coal/oil/gas/cement/flaring across ALL combustion, not just power generation).

data.notes: Record high; ~66% of global power-sector CO2 emissions despite coal supplying only ~36% of generation that year, reflecting coal's higher carbon intensity per kWh generated.

data.category: Natural gas- and oil-fired electricity generation (combined)
data.source: derived from Ember - Global Electricity Review 2024
data.notes: Derived as a residual: total power-sector CO2 (14,153 MtCO2) minus coal-fired CO2 (9,450 MtCO2), both directly reported by Ember. Covers natural gas (~22% of global generation) and oil (~3%); a public source giving the gas/oil split in absolute MtCO2 was not located during this research, so the two are combined here rather than estimated separately.
+1% (+135 MtCO2) versus 2022; described by Ember as an all-time high at the time of publication.

data.source: Ember - Global Electricity Review 2025 (via Carbon Brief)
data.notes: New all-time high, +1.6% year-on-year, even though renewables and nuclear supplied 80% of the growth in generation. IEA's own Electricity 2025 report gives a lower figure (~13,800 MtCO2 for 2024), reflecting scope/methodology differences between the two organizations (see caveats).

data.category: Coal share of global electricity generation
data.notes: Coal-fired generation reached a new volume high of ~10,700 TWh even as its share of the mix fell to the lowest level since the IEA's founding in 1974.

data.category: Natural gas share of global electricity generation
data.notes: Second-largest generation source for more than two decades running; gas-fired generation rose by about 2.5% year-on-year in 2024.

data.category: Oil share of global electricity generation
data.notes: IEA describes oil-fired power as generating 'just a few percent' of the global total; 2% is an approximate mid-point, not an exact reported figure.

data.category: Renewables + nuclear electricity generation (near-zero direct CO2)
data.notes: First year on record that these near-zero-direct-emission sources together crossed 40% of global generation. Renewables alone supplied ~32% (hydropower 14%, wind 8%, solar PV 7%, bioenergy & waste 3%); nuclear supplied the remaining ~9%. 'Near-zero direct' means smokestack/combustion CO2 is effectively zero; full life-cycle emissions (manufacturing, mining, construction) are small but non-zero and are not represented here.

data.category: Carbon intensity of global electricity generation
data.notes: The cleanest average kWh of electricity on record at the time (since at least 2000).

data.category: Carbon intensity of global electricity generation
data.notes: IEA forecasts this intensity declining at ~3.7% per year on average, reaching roughly 415 gCO2/kWh by 2026.

provenance.notes: Revised version, March 2025. Source for the 2024 electricity generation mix (coal/gas/oil/renewables/nuclear shares), coal generation volume, and total energy-related CO2 context.
Used for cross-checking the power sector's role in the 2023 emissions increase and the coal-to-gas switching narrative in advanced economies.
Source for 2023 absolute power-sector CO2 emissions, the coal-fired power CO2 figure, and 2023 carbon intensity of generation.
Source (via Carbon Brief's reporting) for the 2024 total power-sector CO2 figure.

provenance.source_name: Carbon Brief - 'Power-sector CO2 hits all-time high in 2024 despite record growth for clean energy'
provenance.notes: Secondary analysis of Ember's Global Electricity Review 2025 data; used for the 2024 generation-mix percentages (coal 34.4%/10,602 TWh, gas 22%/6,788 TWh) as a cross-check against the IEA figures.

Source for the 2024 carbon intensity of global electricity generation (445 gCO2/kWh) and the IEA's own (lower) power-sector CO2 total for 2024 (~13,800 MtCO2), noted here as a methodology cross-check against Ember's figure.

caveats: Two different organizations (IEA and Ember) publish global power-sector CO2 totals using different plant boundaries, regional coverage, and estimation methods; their totals for the same year differ by several percent (e.g. ~13.8 GtCO2 per IEA's Electricity 2025 report vs. ~14.6 GtCO2 per Ember's Global Electricity Review 2025, both for 2024). Both are included here, clearly labeled by source, rather than reconciled into one 'true' number. The 'natural gas- and oil-fired' row is a derived residual (total minus coal), not a directly published figure, because no source located during this research broke out gas-fired vs. oil-fired CO2 in absolute terms globally -- only their generation SHARES (%) are directly reported. 'Near-zero direct CO2' for renewables and nuclear refers only to combustion/smokestack emissions at the point of generation; it excludes life-cycle emissions from manufacturing, mining, plant construction, and fuel supply chains, which are small but nonzero and vary significantly by technology. This dataset covers only the electricity & heat generation sector; it should not be confused with co2_by_fuel_type.json in this directory, which reports the Global Carbon Project's economy-wide coal/oil/gas/cement/flaring breakdown spanning ALL combustion sectors (transport, industry, buildings, power, etc.), not power generation alone -- the two are conceptually different slices of the data and their category totals are not comparable line-for-line.
